implementation_notes: Ruby ships no named identity function — neither core nor standard library defines a pre-built callable returning its argument — so the classic id structure collapses into method-object idioms around Kernel#itself (added in Ruby 2.2, returns the receiver): :itself.to_proc (per-symbol cached by Symbol#to_proc) is the canonical identity where a block or callable is expected (group_by(&:itself), sort_by(&:itself)), method(:itself) yields a Method object usable in iterators via Method#to_proc, and ->(x) { x } is the explicit lambda for composition slots. Since Ruby 2.6, Proc#>>/Proc#<< compose callables, so an empty-composition base case reduces to the identity proc exactly like fold's neutral element. A hand-written shared constant (IDENTITY = :itself.to_proc) is still justified when a named, reusable identity travels across call sites, because Ruby's block-oriented culture favours passing blocks and symbols over pre-defined function objects.
code_sketch:
IDENTITY = :itself.to_proc               # Kernel#itself (Ruby 2.2+) as a callable
identity = ->(x) { x }                   # explicit lambda form
%w[pear apple pear].group_by(&:itself)   # => {"pear"=>[pear, pear], "apple"=>[apple]}
# neutral element of callable composition (Proc#>>/<<, Ruby 2.6+)
fns = [:upcase.to_proc, ->(s) { s + "!" }]
fns.reduce(identity) { |acc, fn| fn >> acc }.call("hi")  # => "HI!"
pitfalls: method(:itself) binds the Method object to the current receiver: 5.method(:itself).call('x') returns 5, not 'x' — the bound receiver wins over the argument, so this form silently ignores its input and must only be used where returning the receiver is the intent.

Procs and lambdas differ on arity: a regular proc silently discards extra arguments and fills missing ones with nil, while a lambda raises ArgumentError — the wrong-arity identity trap is only caught when the identity is written as ->(x) { x } (strict), not as proc { |x| x }.

&nil in a block pass means 'no block at all', not an identity block — a decorator slot that holds nil and forwards it with &decorator drops the block instead of passing values through, conflating 'absent' with 'identity'.

Each ->(x) { x } written inline allocates a fresh Proc on every evaluation and MRI does not inline identity calls away like Haskell or V8; prefer the cached :itself.to_proc or a shared constant in hot paths, and profile before adding identity layers to per-element loops.

There is no canonical stdlib name, so codebases grow competing local identities (NOOP, IDENTITY_LAMBDA, inline ->(x){x}); standardize on one shared constant to keep call sites greppable and refactoring safe.
sources: https://ruby-doc.org/3.3.0/Symbol.html — Symbol#to_proc: Proc calling the named method on the first parameter.
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/59115314/is-there-an-identity-function-in-ruby — no identity function in Ruby core/stdlib; Object#itself and method(:itself) as nearest forms.
